```ruby
group :development do
```

values.language_tooling_setup:
[clojure-lsp](https://clojure-lsp.io) computes the classpath with
`clojure -Spath`, so it reads the locked downloads when the editor's
environment has `.clojure-cli-purifier/bin` first on `PATH`, such as
through direnv. In a project with a `bb.edn`, clojure-lsp asks babashka for
the classpath, and `.lsp/config.edn` points it at `deps.edn`:

```clojure
{:project-specs [{:project-path "deps.edn"
                  :classpath-cmd ["clojure" "-A:test" "-Spath"]}]}
```

clojure-lsp analyzes the jars on the classpath, which hold the Clojure
sources, and needs no other download.
values.quickstart:
nix shell \
  'github:nix-purifiers/clojure-cli-purifier#clojure' \
  'github:nix-purifiers/clojure-cli-purifier#cli'
clojure-cli-purifier lock \
  --build '-T:build uber' --test '-M:test'
clojure-cli-purifier prefetch
export PATH="$PWD/.clojure-cli-purifier/bin:$PATH"
clojure -T:build uber
clojure -M:test

project is restored, so a language server that reads a project through

downloads need the network.

values.language_tooling_setup:
Editors and language servers find `elm`, `elm-test` and `elm-format` on
`PATH`, and the packages through `ELM_HOME`. The tools in
`elm-stuff/elm-purifier/bin` set `ELM_HOME` themselves, so putting that
directory first on `PATH` is all an editor needs. The same directory holds
`elm-language-server`, which runs the language server with that `PATH`:

```zsh
PATH="$PWD/elm-stuff/elm-purifier/bin:$PATH" code .
```

With direnv, the line `PATH_add elm-stuff/elm-purifier/bin` in `.envrc`
does the same. The language server sometimes hangs while it starts, and
restarting it from the editor fixes that.
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/elm-purifier'
elm-purifier lock
elm-purifier prefetch
export PATH="$PWD/elm-stuff/elm-purifier/bin:$PATH"
elm make src/Main.elm
elm-test

Editors such as Metals (in VS Code) and IntelliJ IDEA talk to Mill through
the Build Server Protocol (BSP), and start Mill with the command in
`.bsp/mill-bsp.json`. Write that file through the purifier:

from the lockfile. The lock run starts Mill's BSP server and asks it what
an editor asks first (the build targets and the sources of their
dependencies), so the server's own libraries and the source jars an editor
shows are in the lock. The script names the mill-purifier package it was
written by; run the install again after updating mill-purifier.

```zsh
opam-purifier lock --tool ocaml-lsp-server --tool ocamlformat
```

versions, and the Nix build leaves them out. `prefetch` installs them into
`_opam`, and `source .opam-purifier/env.sh` puts `ocamllsp` and
`ocamlformat` on `PATH`. Start the editor from that environment, or from
direnv. The server runs offline.

nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/opam-purifier'
opam-purifier lock
opam-purifier prefetch
source .opam-purifier/env.sh
dune build
dune test

values.language_tooling_setup:
Editors and language servers, such as pyright, read the project's virtual
environment, which the offline install fills like any other `poetry
install`. They download nothing.

setuptools installs an editable path dependency through an import hook by
default, which pyright and other type checkers do not follow. This happens
with or without the purifier. Poetry can ask setuptools for its compat mode
instead, which writes a plain path entry, in the project's `poetry.toml`:

```toml
[installer.build-config-settings.<package>]
editable_mode = "compat"
```
values.quickstart:
nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/poetry-purifier'
poetry purifier lock
poetry purifier prefetch
poetry install
eval "$(poetry env activate)"
pytest

scala-cli-purifier.summary: Locked, Nix-resolved dependencies for Scala CLI.

values.language_tooling_setup:
```zsh
scala-cli setup-ide .
```

run through the wrapper, configures Metals, or any other editor that speaks
the Build Server Protocol, to build the project offline on the prefetched
downloads: it points the launch command in `.bsp/scala-cli.json` at the
wrapper, which starts scala-cli's build server with the locked cache and
the offline mirror. Run it again after `lock`.

The lock run opens the project the way an editor does, and compiles it on
the Bloop compilation server that serves an editor, so the lockfile holds
what an editor asks for, such as the source jars of the dependencies and
the compiler bridge of Bloop. `lock --no-ide` locks without them, for a
smaller lockfile.

values.language_tooling_setup:
The toolchains include ZLS. After a `prefetch`, ZLS finds every package
where zig would, also offline, so go-to-definition on an `@import` of a
dependency opens the locked package. Point the editor at the `zls` of the
toolchain, so it matches the zig version of the lock.

nix shell 'github:nix-purifiers/zig-purifier#toolchain-zig_0_15'
zig-purifier lock
zig build
zig build test

native.text: Prerequisites: {facts.runtime_requirements}.
Commit the lockfiles: {facts.lockfiles}.
Locking excludes `{facts.generated_cache_directory}` from the native build context. Also commit the updated ignore file.
The native lock records exact revisions; its companion records artifact hashes, original metadata, and resolution configuration.
OCI manifest, configuration, and layer identities retain their native SHA-256 digests. The lock adds platform selections and input fingerprints.

fresh.text:
Run `{commands.lock}` after changing dependency declarations. Relocking resolves dependencies again; it does not retain existing pins.

Run `{commands.prefetch}` before building.
Update one selected dependency with `{commands.named-update} {facts.named_update_example}`. Other selected pins are retained.

locked.text:
Run `{commands.lock}` after changing dependency declarations. Relocking retains existing pins.

Run `{commands.update}` to update dependencies, then `{commands.prefetch}`.
Update one selected dependency with `{commands.named-update} {facts.named_update_example}`. Other selected pins are retained.

native.text: Keep using the native build and test commands in your working tree. After changing dependency declarations, refresh the lock through the native lock workflow shown above.
Relocking retains existing pins.
The development environment supplies the native tools and their purifier integration. Use that environment for builds, tests, and editor processes so they share the selected dependencies.
Without an applicable lock, the integration warns and runs the ordinary native tool.
The native tool reads the prepared project dependencies directly; wrapper activation is not required.

wrapper.text: The shell supplies a wrapper for the native build tool. Without an applicable lock, it warns and runs the ordinary native tool. A stale or invalid lock fails with a repair command.
The supplied wrapper is required for native builds.
The integration handles {facts.supported_native_commands}; other native commands run normally.

Alternatively, activate the native plugin in the build. Resolve `{facts.native_plugin_coordinate}` from the [native plugin repository]({facts.native_plugin_repository}). Keep bootstrap dependencies separate from application dependencies.
Native Maven bootstrap resolution is impure; use the wrapper for pure plugin resolution.

native.text: Prepare dependencies using the Quickstart workflow before disconnecting. The lock covers the recorded dependency downloads; downloads performed outside that lock need separate inputs.

scoped.text:
Run `{commands.prefetch}` to prepare the locked dependencies. This does not guarantee that the entire build can run offline.

Outside this lock: {facts.offline_limits}.
Prefetch retains {facts.prefetch_components} through garbage-collector roots beside the selected lockfile.

command.text: Configure the Language Server Protocol (LSP) client to launch `{commands.editor}` from the development shell. This puts its language tooling in the same environment as the native build.
Diagnostics and definition lookup work offline after prefetch.
The language server can retrieve source code for locked dependencies.
The launcher prepares Eclipse project metadata with immutable dependency and source JAR paths.
